📸 My view of Lake Superior from atop the massive sand dune that's just west of Grand Marais, At the bottom of the dune, you may notice a group of ant-sized people walking the water's edge. Taken with my iPhone 4s in August, 2012 💙 🧡

My friend and I used to venture out on this rocky stretch to stand above the water and look out. I’d always get nervous and stop when the rocks became crooked and jagged, while my friend would race on ahead, eager to explore. I hope that going forward, I can find the confidence and the courage that my friend has always shown, and be able to embody those traits myself soon.

Trying to navigate from a when your eyes are two feet off the water can be tough. It took me almost an hour to find the passage through the grass to the north channel of the Naiscoot River in , including a false start up a beaver channel. It wasn't until I got out and stood higher up that I could see where the passage might be.

We stopped at Two Harbors on the way north for lunch and a splash in Lake Superior. Everyone enjoyed scrambling on the rocks and exploring the little tide pools. Tonttu got a full immersion baptism in the waters of Gitche Gumee: he hopped down a small cliff into what he thought was shallow water and ended up over his head! Good thing he was wearing his harness and could get some help being hauled back up to dry land.
For those of you who don't know, pretty much sits on a hillside along . When we get heavy , we can get scenes like this as water flows down the and towards the lake. for the continues until 10 p.m.

Finally down to the lake! The trail parallels the water a little ways inland, so you have to follow occasional spur trails to get down to the water. Zeena definitely enjoyed poking around the waves and rocky tide pools much more than Tonttu, who preferred to snuffle for dead things in the pebbled beach up from the water.
Down by the big lakes shoreline to cool down and read. It is suspiciously empty, I do wonder if the wind is blowing the warm water away from shore...
The full view out to from atop a sand dune. The water at the bottom left is a creek that is naturally dammed up when the water is low.

The wind turbine is no longer there (it aged out) & not all of the reactors are currently online. The green at the foot of the turbine & to its left are hiking trails, including a boardwalk over a marsh. Along the beach are picnic tables and playgrounds. Along the shoreline to its west, not seen here, is a paved trail that winds along the lake for a very long way. This image was taken from East Point Park, so suffers from some hazy distortion.

Years ago I owned a remote piece of property on Sleeping Bay of Lake Superior. This is in the western part of the Michigan UP. One year I drove as close as I could get, hiked from there, waded chest deep to cross the West Fork of the Sleeping River and then went for a balmy swim in the lake. The bay is relatively shallow and has a hard sand bottom. When there is an onshore breeze the warm surface water is pushed into the bay. I could have played in the water all afternoon.

Seen upon my repatriation: calling the edges of the “coasts.” They’re inland shores NOT geologic boundaries between continents and oceans. It’s laughable real estate speak having a West & South Coast, ruining ever more unaffordable land, destroying vital habitat & resources.
